unit.title: Comply with the occupational health and safety, security and hygiene practices

summary: This unit teaches you to work safely, securely and hygienically in a villa or hotel. You will learn the duties of employers and workers, how to find hazards and control risks, how to lift and move safely, handle chemicals, prevent and fight fires, give first aid, protect guests and their belongings, and keep yourself, your work area and food clean. You will also learn how to report accidents and how to act in emergencies such as hurricanes and earthquakes.

blocks.p: A villa or hotel is a workplace and also someone's holiday home. Guests expect to be safe, to have their belongings protected and to be served clean food and clean rooms. Workers expect to go home without injury. Both depend on everyone following the same safe habits every day. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. It covers three linked areas: **health and safety** (preventing injury and illness), **security** (protecting people and property) and **hygiene** (preventing the spread of germs).

What this means in a villa or hotel
rows: Know the duties of the employer and the worker
Follow the rules, use PPE, report hazards and accidents
Know what the property must provide
Find hazards and control risks
Spot slips, trips, chemicals, electrical faults and heavy loads
Use the hierarchy of control and a simple risk assessment
Work safely with people, loads and equipment
Lift and carry safely; use ladders and trolleys
Avoid heat illness
Handle chemicals, waste, sharps and body fluids safely
Read labels and SDS; dilute and store correctly
Deal with glass, needles and spills
Prevent and respond to fire
Know the fire triangle and the right extinguisher
Raise the alarm and evacuate
Give first aid and report accidents
Make the area safe, call for help, give basic first aid
Fill in an accident report
Keep guests and property secure
Control keys, check identity and protect privacy
Report suspicious people and items
Keep clean and hygienic
Wash your hands, keep food safe and cool
Clean and disinfect correctly
Respond to emergencies
Know what to do in a hurricane, earthquake, gas leak or power cut

flow: Spot the hazard
Judge the risk
Control it
Tell the team
Check it works
Report and review

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks. In the practical tasks you inspect a training guest room, kitchen and front desk, write a risk assessment, and carry out emergency exercises (a fire evacuation, burn first aid and a front desk security check). The assessor watches how you work as well as what you write.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Never put yourself in danger to deal with a hazard. If you are not trained, or it is not safe, move away, warn others and report it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Both** the employer and every worker. They work together, for example in staff briefings or on a safety committee. Jamaica's laws and the property's own rules set out these duties.

head: The employer must
The worker must
rows: Provide a safe place and safe ways of working
Keep the building, equipment and electrical items in repair
Provide PPE, safe chemicals with safety data sheets, training and supervision
Provide first-aid kits, fire equipment and clear emergency plans
Find hazards, assess risks and put controls in place
Record and look into accidents
Take care of their own safety and that of co-workers and guests
Follow the rules and training they have been given
Use PPE and equipment as shown; never remove guards
Report hazards, faults, accidents and near misses at once
Not come to work under the influence of alcohol or drugs
Co-operate with the employer

blocks.p: A **hazard** is anything that could cause harm, such as a wet floor, a cleaning chemical or a frayed cable. **Risk** is the chance that the hazard will cause harm, and how bad the harm would be. A wet floor in a corridor nobody uses is a small risk. The same wet floor in the lobby at check-in is a larger one.

head: Hazard
Who could be harmed and how
Common control
rows: Wet floor
Anyone: slips and falls
Dry it; wet floor sign; non-slip shoes
Cleaning chemical
Room attendant: burns, fumes
Read the label; dilute correctly; gloves; ventilation
Frayed cable
Anyone: electric shock, fire
Stop using; tag it; report it
Heavy linen bag
Worker: back injury
Smaller loads; trolley; team lift
Broken glass
Worker and guests: cuts
Gloves; dustpan and brush; sharps or glass box
Hot oil and steam
Cook: burns and scalds
Keep handles in; careful lifting; PPE
Pool
Children and weak swimmers: drowning
Fence and gate; supervision; rescue equipment; clear rules

blocks.p: Controls are chosen in order, from best to last.

head: Order
Control
Example
rows: **Eliminate** the hazard: remove it completely
Remove a broken chair or a loose rug
**Substitute**: use something safer
Use a milder cleaner instead of a strong acid
**Engineering controls**: guards, ventilation, equipment
Fit a guard on a slicer; use a trolley instead of carrying
**Administrative controls**: rules, training, signs, rosters
Wet floor sign; training; a rota for lifting
**PPE**: protective equipment worn by the person
Gloves, goggles, non-slip shoes

blocks.note: PPE is the **last line of defence** because it only protects the person wearing it, and only if it is worn and used correctly. Always try to remove or reduce the hazard first.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Find the hazards in the task
Decide who might be harmed and how
Judge the risk (low, medium or high) and choose controls
Write down the findings and tell the team
Review when something changes or after an accident

blocks.h: PPE for housekeeping and kitchen work

head: Task
PPE and reason
rows: Cleaning toilets and bathrooms with chemicals
Rubber gloves and eye protection if the label says: stops burns and splashes
Kitchen work
Closed, non-slip shoes: prevent slips and protect feet from hot spills; apron; oven cloths for hot trays
Handling broken glass or waste
Thick gloves; tongs for sharps
Spilled blood or vomit
Disposable gloves and an apron
Laundry and heavy lifting
Closed shoes; gloves if needed

blocks.note: Report hazards, accidents and **near misses**. A near miss is an incident where nobody was hurt but someone could have been. Fixing the cause before someone is hurt is the whole point of reporting.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Safe movement: lifting, slips, ladders, electricity and heat

flow: Think: how heavy and awkward is the load, and where is it going?
Test one corner; get help or a trolley if it is too heavy
Clear the route and open doors
Stand close, feet apart, one slightly forward
Bend your knees, keep your back straight, firm grip
Lift smoothly with the legs; keep the load close
Turn by moving your feet, never by twisting your back
Lower by bending the knees

ul: In a **team lift**, one person gives the commands and everyone lifts together.
Do not overfill laundry bags. Keep heavy items on low shelves.
Report back pain early.

head: Cause
Control
rows: Wet floors
Mop in sections; put out a wet floor sign; dry the floor; do not leave it until it is dry
Spills in the kitchen
Wipe up at once; non-slip shoes; report grease on the floor
Boxes and trolleys in corridors
Keep corridors and exits clear; move boxes to their place or report them
Cables across the floor
Tidy or cover; never run a cable across a wet floor
Poor lighting
Report broken lights; never work in the dark

ul: Use a **step ladder in good condition** to reach high shelves, not a chair, box or bed.
Check the feet are firm and level and that the legs are fully open and locked.
Face the ladder, keep three points of contact (two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand), and do not over-reach.
Have another person hold the ladder where needed.

head: Hazard
What to do
rows: Frayed cable, damaged plug or sparking socket
Stop using the item, unplug it only if it is safe, tag it 'Do not use' and report it
Wet hands near plugs and switches
Dry your hands first. Water conducts electricity and can cause a shock
Overloaded sockets
Do not plug many items into one socket or extension
Equipment near water
Keep dryers and cables away from sinks, pools and wet floors
Repairs
Never repair electrical equipment yourself. Report it to maintenance

blocks.note: **Lockout-tagout** means locking or switching a faulty machine off and fixing a warning label to it so that nobody can use it until a trained person repairs it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V (220 V for some larger equipment) at 50 Hz. Do not plug equipment into a socket it was not made for. Extension cords across wet floors, around pools and in kitchens are a common cause of shocks.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Kitchens, laundries and outdoor work in Jamaica's heat can cause heat illness.

head: Condition
Signs
What to do
rows: Heat exhaustion
Heavy sweating, pale and clammy skin, headache, dizziness, nausea, tiredness, fast pulse
Move to a cool place, lie down with legs raised, loosen clothing, give sips of cool water, cool the skin with a damp cloth; get medical help if no better
Heat stroke (an emergency)
Hot, dry or very sweaty skin, confusion, fainting, very high body temperature
Call for emergency help at once; cool the person as much as possible; do not give drinks if unconscious

ul: Drink water often, before you feel thirsty.
Take short breaks in a cool place.
Wear light, loose uniform where the rules allow.
Report a colleague who seems unwell.

sections.title: Chemicals, waste, sharps and body fluids

flow: Read the label and the safety data sheet (SDS)
Put on the PPE the label asks for
Measure and dilute exactly as the label says, with a marked jug
Work with good ventilation
Use the chemical, close the lid, and return it to the store
Clean up spills at once as the SDS says
Wash your hands

blocks.p: The **SDS** (safety data sheet) comes from the supplier. It gives the hazards, PPE, first aid, firefighting, spill and storage information for a chemical. Keep the SDS where staff can find it.

head: Rule
Why
rows: Never mix chemicals, especially bleach with ammonia or acid toilet cleaners
They give off a toxic gas
Keep chemicals in their **original labelled containers**, or correctly labelled spray bottles
Someone could swallow or misuse an unlabelled product; the warnings are lost
Never put chemicals in drink bottles or food containers
A guest or child may drink them
Dilute exactly as the label says
Too weak will not work; too strong can burn skin and damage surfaces
Store in a cool, dry, locked, ventilated place, off the floor, away from food
Prevents spills, fire and contamination
Keep the trolley's chemicals away from clean linen and guest supplies, and never leave the trolley where children can reach it
Prevents contamination and poisoning

head: Accident
First action
rows: Chemical in the eye
Flush with plenty of clean, cool water for several minutes and get medical help
Chemical on skin
Remove contaminated clothing; rinse with plenty of water; get help if it burns or irritates
Breathing fumes
Move to fresh air; get help if you feel dizzy or have trouble breathing
Spill
Keep people away; follow the SDS; wear PPE; contain and clean up; report it

blocks.note: Pool chemicals such as chlorine must be stored cool, dry and away from other chemicals, especially acids and fuel. Never mix pool chemicals. Add chemicals to water, not water to chemicals, and follow the label.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Situation
What you do
rows: Broken glass

Keep people away; put on thick gloves; pick up large pieces carefully; sweep up the small pieces and use damp paper for tiny ones; put it in a sharps or glass box or wrap it well. Never use bare hands
A used needle

Do not touch it with your hands or try to recap it. Use tongs to put it in a sharps container, then report it. If you are pricked, let it bleed gently, wash with soap and running water, report it and get medical advice
Blood or vomit
Put on disposable gloves and an apron; cover the spill with a spill kit; scoop it up; clean with detergent, then disinfect as the label says; bag and seal the waste; wash your hands

blocks.note: Treat all blood and body fluids as if they were infectious. Never touch them without gloves, and never pick up sharps with your fingers.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Separate waste as the property requires: general, glass, recycling, food.
Keep bins covered and emptied often, so that they do not attract flies, rats and stray dogs.
Dispose of chemicals, oil, batteries and sharps through the correct routes. Never pour chemicals down drains.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Cleaning
Removing dirt, grease and germs from surfaces with detergent and water. It comes first, because disinfectant cannot work through dirt
Disinfecting
Using a chemical to kill most harmful germs on a clean surface. The surface must stay wet for the contact time on the label
Sterilising
Killing all germs, usually with heat or pressure

blocks.p: A fire needs three things: **heat**, **fuel** and **oxygen**. Take any one away and the fire goes out.

head: Remove
How
Example
rows: Heat
Cool it
Water on a wood or paper fire
Fuel
Take it away
Turn off the gas supply
Oxygen
Smother it
A fire blanket or lid on a pan; a CO2 extinguisher

ul: Keep exits, corridors and stairs clear. A linen trolley must never block an escape route, even for a few minutes.
Do not overload sockets. Report faulty wiring and equipment.
Clean cooker hoods, filters and grease traps. Clean lint from dryer filters.
Store flammable liquids and gas cylinders safely, away from heat.
Never leave cooking unattended.
Do not prop open fire doors.
Know where the fire alarm points, extinguishers and exits are.

blocks.p: Extinguisher colours and names can differ between makers, so always read the label on the extinguisher before you use it. The table gives the usual uses.

head: Extinguisher
Usually used on
Take care
rows: Water
Wood, paper, cloth, linen (ordinary combustibles)
Never on electrical equipment or burning oil or fat
Foam
Ordinary combustibles and flammable liquids
Not on live electrical equipment unless the label says it is safe
Carbon dioxide (CO2)
Electrical fires, such as a computer or switchboard, and flammable liquids
Use with good ventilation; the fire may re-ignite, so watch it afterwards
Dry powder
Mixed fires, flammable liquids and gas, and some electrical fires
Reduces visibility and makes a mess; does not cool well, so the fire may re-ignite
Wet chemical
Cooking oil and fat fires in kitchens
Not for electrical fires

head: Item
Use
rows: Fire blanket
Smother a small pan fire or wrap a person whose clothes are on fire. Kept in a quick-release holder

blocks.note: **Never use water on a cooking oil or electrical fire.** Water on burning oil makes it splash and spread. Water on live electrical equipment can cause a shock.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Pull the pin
Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire
Squeeze the handle
Sweep from side to side

blocks.p: Only fight a fire if it is small, you have been trained, you have a clear way out behind you and the alarm has been raised. If in doubt, **get out**.

flow: Raise the alarm: shout 'Fire!' and use the nearest alarm point
Call the fire brigade (110 in Jamaica) or make sure that someone does
Help guests and staff leave by the nearest safe exit, closing doors behind you
Do not use the lift
Go to the assembly point and take part in the roll call
Do not go back in for any reason

ul: Stop what you are doing. Leave by the nearest safe exit as the fire plan says. Walk, do not run.
Help guests, especially children, older guests and guests with disabilities. Tell your supervisor about anyone who may not have left.
Go to the **assembly point**, a safe place outside where everyone gathers.

blocks.p: Many villas use LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) in cylinders for stoves and water heaters. LPG is heavier than air, so a leak collects low down. If you smell gas: do **not** use switches or flames, open windows and doors, turn off the gas at the cylinder if it is safe, leave the area, keep others out and report it at once.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, dial 110 for the fire brigade or an ambulance. Know the emergency numbers and the property's own address and phone number, and put them by every phone.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Make the area safe so that nobody else is hurt
Check the injured person; do not move them if they may have a back or neck injury
Call the trained first aider
For serious injury, call an ambulance (110 in Jamaica) and ask someone else to call while you stay
Give only the first aid you have been trained to give; wear gloves if there is blood
Keep the person calm and warm
Tell the supervisor and fill in the accident report

head: Injury
First aid
rows: Burn or scald
Cool under cool running water for about 10 to 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter or toothpaste. Cover loosely with a clean non-fluffy dressing. Get medical help for large, deep or face burns
Cut
Press firmly with a clean pad; raise the limb if possible; cover with a dressing; get help if serious
Choking
Encourage coughing; if they cannot breathe or speak, give back blows and abdominal thrusts as trained, and call for help
Heat illness
See the section on heat
Electric shock
Switch off the power if it is safe or use something dry and non-conducting to separate the person; do not touch them while they are connected; call for help
Fainting
Lay the person down with legs raised; check breathing; give fresh air; get help if they do not recover quickly

blocks.note: First aid is the **first** help, not the full treatment. Always call a trained first aider or a doctor for anything serious. Use only the first aid that you have been trained to give.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Fill in the accident book or report form straight away. Write the date, time and place, what happened, who was hurt and how, who saw it, and what first aid was given. The report helps the property find the cause and stop it happening again, and it is evidence if there is a claim.
The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to November. Every property should have a written hurricane plan and train its staff.

head: When
What to do
rows: Before the storm

Follow official warnings and the manager's instructions; bring in or tie down loose items such as pool furniture and umbrellas; fit shutters; check supplies of drinking water, non-perishable food, torches, batteries, first-aid kits, a battery radio and fuel for the generator; protect important papers and computers; tell guests what to expect and where the safe rooms are
During
Stay indoors, away from windows, in the safe area; do not go outside until the all-clear is given
After

Check for hazards before working: fallen power lines (stay well away and report), gas leaks, broken glass, flooding and damaged roofs; photograph and report damage; check food after a power cut and throw it away if it may be unsafe

blocks.p: Jamaica lies in an earthquake zone. If you are indoors: **Drop, Cover and Hold on**. Get down on your hands and knees, cover your head and neck under a sturdy table or beside an inside wall, and hold on. Stay away from windows and heavy furniture. After the shaking stops, check for injuries and fires, switch off gas if you can smell it, and leave by the stairs, not the lift.

ul: Use torches, not candles, where possible.
Keep fridge and freezer doors closed to keep food cold, and check temperatures afterwards.
Know where the generator, the tank and the pump switch are.
Never start a service or cook if you cannot clean up, wash your hands or rinse. Tell your supervisor.

sections.title: Security: protecting guests, property and privacy

blocks.p: Guests must feel safe and know their belongings and information are protected. Every staff member has a part in security.

head: Area
What you do
rows: Guest privacy
Never say a guest's room number aloud or give it to callers or visitors. Offer to connect a call or take a message
Identity checks
Check identity against the registration before giving a replacement key or giving out any information
Key control
Sign master keys in and out; keep them on your body; never lend them; report lost keys at once so that locks or cards can be changed
Rooms
Never let anyone into a room without checking with the front desk; keep the trolley across the open door while cleaning; lock doors when you leave
Documents and cash
Keep registration cards, passports and payment details out of sight and locked away; keep cash in a locked drawer or safe; tell guests about the in-room safe
Lost property
Log every found item and hand it in to lost property; never keep it
Strangers in staff areas
Wear your name badge; ask politely who someone is; report suspicious people

head: Situation
What to do
rows: A stranger with no key inside a guest's room
Stay calm; do not confront them; leave safely if you can and call security or the supervisor
An unattended bag in the lobby
Do not touch it; keep people away; report it to security
A person tries to get a key without ID
Politely decline; check ID; call the supervisor
A guest reports something stolen
Be calm and polite; note the details; tell the supervisor; do not accuse anyone

blocks.note: Never put yourself in danger to protect property. People matter more than things. Call security or the police and give clear facts.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **CCTV** (closed-circuit television) cameras help to deter and investigate crime. They are used in public areas such as entrances and corridors, not in guest rooms or bathrooms. Keep logs of keys, visitors, lost property and incidents accurately.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, guests' personal details are protected under the data protection law. Keep guest records private and secure, and share them only with staff who need them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Bathe daily, keep nails short and clean, and wear a clean uniform each shift.
Food handlers wear no nail polish, keep hair tied back and covered, and wear little or no jewellery.
Do not eat, smoke or chew gum while handling food.
Cover cuts with a **blue waterproof plaster**, which is easy to see if it falls into food, and wear a glove over it if working with food.
Anyone with diarrhoea, vomiting or a skin infection must tell the supervisor and stay away from food until allowed back.
In Jamaica food handlers must hold a Food Handler's Permit from the health department.

flow: Wet hands with warm running water
Apply soap
Rub palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and under nails for at least 20 seconds
Rinse well
Dry with a clean paper towel
Turn off the tap with the towel

head: Wash your hands
Because
rows: Before work and before handling food
Germs from outside can get into food
After the toilet
Germs from faeces spread easily
After handling raw meat, bins, money or chemicals
Raw food and bins carry harmful germs
After coughing, sneezing or touching your face
Germs from your nose and mouth spread to food
After cleaning toilets or handling dirty linen (housekeeping)
Stops spread to guests and clean linen
Between tasks
Stops cross-contamination

blocks.note: Gloves do not replace hand washing. Wash your hands before putting gloves on and change them often, especially after touching raw food, the bin or your face.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Rule
Why
rows: Keep cold food at **5 °C or below**
Germs grow slowly in the cold
Keep hot food at 63 °C or above, or as the food safety plan says
Germs are slowed or killed by high heat
Cook poultry to a core temperature of at least 74 °C, checked with a clean probe thermometer, or as the plan says
Kills harmful germs inside the meat
Do not leave food in the **danger zone**, between about 5 °C and 63 °C, for more than about two hours in total
Germs grow fastest here
Keep raw meat and ready-to-eat foods apart, with separate boards and knives
Stops germs passing from raw food to food that will not be cooked again
Use older stock first: **FIFO** (first in, first out); check dates
Stops food going out of date
Cover, label and date stored food
So that it is used in time and not contaminated
Keep pests out; store food off the floor
Pests carry germs

blocks.note: Many villas serve guests in the heat of the day, at buffets on a terrace or at the pool. Keep cold food on ice or in the fridge and hot food hot. Do not leave a buffet in the sun, and bring out small amounts at a time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Remove waste and food
Clean with detergent and hot water
Rinse
Disinfect and leave for the contact time
Rinse if the label says
Dry or leave to air-dry
Wash your hands

ul: I can say what the employer and the worker must do for safety.
I can explain hazard and risk, and give examples from a villa.
I can list the hierarchy of control and say why PPE is the last line of defence.
I can carry out a simple risk assessment and report hazards, accidents and near misses.
I can lift and carry safely, and use a ladder or a trolley properly.
I can deal with a wet floor, a trailing cable and a blocked exit.
I can recognise heat illness and give first aid.
I can read a label and SDS, dilute a chemical and store it safely.
I can explain why chemicals are never mixed or kept in drink bottles.
I can clear broken glass, a needle, blood or vomit safely.
I can name the parts of the fire triangle and choose the right extinguisher.
I can use PASS and know when not to fight a fire.
I can raise the alarm and lead guests to the assembly point.
I can give first aid for a burn and fill in an accident report.
I can say what to do in a hurricane, an earthquake or a gas leak.
I can protect guests' privacy and keys, check identity and report suspicious people or bags.
I can wash my hands properly and keep food safe, using temperature, FIFO and separation.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the action and the reason. For example: 'I wear rubber gloves, because the cleaner can burn my skin.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The chance that a hazard will cause harm, and how bad the harm would be.
Personal protective equipment, such as gloves, goggles and non-slip shoes.
An incident in which nobody was hurt but someone could have been.
Safety data sheet: the supplier's sheet of hazards, first aid and storage for a chemical.
The order for controlling risks: eliminate, substitute, engineer, administer, PPE.
Lifting, carrying and moving loads by hand.
Locking a faulty machine off and tagging it so nobody can use it.
Heat, fuel and oxygen: the three things a fire needs.
A fire-resistant cloth in a quick-release holder, used to smother a small fire.
Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep: how to use an extinguisher.
A safe place outside where everyone gathers after leaving a building.
The planned, orderly way of getting everyone out of a building.
Liquefied petroleum gas, kept in cylinders and heavier than air.
The first help given to an injured or ill person before a doctor or ambulance.
Needles, broken glass and other items that can cut or prick.
A key that opens many rooms; it must be signed out and never lent.
How long a surface must stay wet with disinfectant for it to work.
The range of temperatures, about 5 °C to 63 °C, where germs in food grow fastest.
First in, first out: using older stock first.
Passing germs from one food, surface or person to another.

c1.title: A burning smell in the laundry at Runaway Bay
c1.text: Delano, a laundry attendant at a villa in Runaway Bay, smells burning near the tumble dryer. He sees small flames and smoke behind the dryer, where the plug and cable are, and lint around the back. Two other staff are working in the next room and guests are at the pool. The building has an alarm point in the corridor, a CO2 extinguisher and a water extinguisher by the door.

c2.title: New cleaning products at a Kingston guest house
c2.text: A guest house in Kingston has a new delivery of cleaning chemicals. A new room attendant, Shanelle, finds that a spray bottle on her trolley has no label. A colleague, Orville, suggests mixing the bleach with the toilet cleaner in one bucket 'to clean twice as fast'. Later Shanelle spills some of the strong cleaner on the bathroom floor and starts to feel dizzy from the smell.

c3.title: A very hot day in the laundry and kitchen
c3.text: On a very hot afternoon in a villa near Treasure Beach, the laundry is full. Kimani has been lifting 20 kg wet linen bags without a break for three hours. He has stopped drinking water because the bathroom is far away. Now he feels dizzy, has a headache, is sweating heavily and his skin is pale and clammy. A co-worker, Alecia, notices.

c4.title: Front desk security in Montego Bay
c4.text: At the front desk of a hotel in Montego Bay, Sandra gets a call from a man who says he is a friend of a guest and asks for her room number. Later a woman says she is the guest's sister and asks for a key so she can 'get something from the room'. Sandra has no booking record for the woman. Housekeeper Devon also finds a gold chain on a bathroom shelf when cleaning a room after check-out.

c5.title: A buffet lunch at a Negril villa
c5.text: A villa in Negril serves a self-serve buffet on a sunny terrace for a birthday party. Chicken and rice have been out for over three hours in the sun. The potato salad has been on the table since the start and now feels warm. The cook, Marlon, has a small cut on his finger and wears no plaster. A helper cuts raw chicken and then slices tomatoes on the same board.

questions.q: What should Delano do first?
o: Pour a bucket of water on the dryer and the plug to put out the flames
Raise the alarm and get people out, then call 110
Pick up the dryer cable and try to pull the plug from the wall
Finish the load that is in the dryer and then report the smell
questions.why: The first priority is people's safety: raise the alarm and evacuate, and call the fire brigade. Water on electrical equipment can cause a shock, pulling a burning plug is dangerous, and delay lets the fire grow.

questions.q: If Delano is trained and the fire is still small with a clear exit behind him, which extinguisher is best?
o: The CO2 extinguisher
The water extinguisher beside the door
A bucket of sand from the garden
A wet towel from the laundry
questions.why: CO2 does not conduct electricity and leaves no residue, so it is suitable for electrical fires. Water and wet towels can cause a shock. If the fire grows, he should leave.

questions.q: After everyone has left the laundry, where should staff and guests go?
o: Back to their rooms to collect their valuables
To the pool, where it is safe and cool
To the car park, then back inside to check the dryer
To the assembly point, for a roll call
questions.why: Everyone goes to the assembly point so that the supervisor can count them and tell the fire brigade if anyone is missing. Nobody goes back in until it is declared safe.

questions.q: Which habit would best prevent a fire like this one in the future?
o: Running the dryer for as long as possible on every load
Keeping the dryer pushed tightly against the wall
Cleaning the lint out and reporting a damaged plug
Leaving the plug in the wall socket when the dryer is not in use
questions.why: Lint is fuel and will catch fire easily, so it must be cleaned out regularly. A damaged plug must be reported and not used. Tight spacing and long drying times make heat build up.

questions.q: What should Shanelle do about the spray bottle with no label?
o: Smell it to find out what it contains, then use it if it seems familiar
Use it on the bathroom floor first to see what it does
Not use it, and tell her supervisor
Top it up with water and carry on using it
questions.why: Unlabelled containers hide the hazards and the correct PPE. Never smell or test an unknown chemical. Report it and have the contents identified and labelled or disposed of.

questions.q: Why is Orville's idea of mixing bleach with toilet cleaner dangerous?
o: The mixture will leave white marks on the surfaces
The mixture can give off a toxic gas
The mixture will be too weak to clean properly
The mixture will cost the guest house more money
questions.why: Mixing bleach with acid toilet cleaners (or ammonia) can release toxic gas that harms the lungs and eyes. Never mix chemicals unless the label says it is safe.

questions.q: Shanelle spills the strong cleaner and feels dizzy. What should she do first?
o: Move to fresh air and tell her supervisor
Mop up the spill quickly, because the smell will soon fade
Close the bathroom door and carry on with the next room
Sit down in the bathroom until the dizziness goes away
questions.why: Dizziness from fumes means she should leave the area for fresh air and report it. The spill is then dealt with using the SDS and PPE, with the area ventilated.

questions.q: Where can Shanelle find out the correct first aid, PPE and storage for the cleaner?
o: From the price list that the supplier sent with the delivery
From a guest who says he has used the product at home before
From the colour of the liquid and the smell of the product
On the label and on the safety data sheet (SDS)
questions.why: The label and the SDS give the hazards, PPE, first aid, spill and storage information. Price lists, guests, colour and smell are not reliable sources of safety information.

questions.q: Which condition is most likely for Kimani?
o: A cold from the air conditioning
A back strain from lifting
Hunger because he skipped lunch
Heat exhaustion
questions.why: Heavy sweating, pale and clammy skin, headache and dizziness in a hot workplace are signs of heat exhaustion, made worse by lack of water and heavy work.

questions.q: What should Alecia do first?
o: Tell him to splash his face and then carry on lifting the linen bags
Give him a cup of strong coffee so that he wakes up and feels better
Move him somewhere cool, sit him down and give sips of water
Ask him to keep working so that the laundry is not late for the guests
questions.why: He needs to cool down, rest and drink. Caffeine and more work would make it worse. If he does not improve, or becomes confused or faints, call for emergency help.

questions.q: Which change would best protect Kimani and others next time?
o: Wearing heavier clothing so that he sweats more and feels cooler
Lighter loads, a trolley, breaks and water close by
Working faster so that the heavy work is done sooner
Drinking only when he feels thirsty and the laundry is empty
questions.why: Controls are rest breaks, water, smaller loads and equipment. Waiting for thirst is too late, and extra clothing or speed makes heat illness more likely.

questions.q: What should Sandra say to the man who asks for the guest's room number?
o: Offer to connect the call, without giving the room number
Give the room number, as the caller says he is a friend
Ask him which floor the room is on and confirm if he is right
Tell him the number once he has given his own name and phone number
questions.why: A guest's room number is private information. Offering to put the call through, or take a message, lets the guest decide whether to speak to the caller.

questions.q: The woman says she is the guest's sister and asks for a key. What is the best response?
o: Politely explain the rule and phone the guest
Give her the key, as it is only for a short time
Ask her to wait in the room until the guest returns
Let her go up with a housekeeper to collect the item
questions.why: Keys are given only to the registered guest after checking identity. Phoning the guest, or asking the supervisor, handles the request safely without causing offence.

questions.q: What should Devon do with the gold chain?
o: Keep it safely in his pocket until the guest asks about it
Leave it where it was found, in case the guest comes back
Give it to the next guest who checks in to the room
Log it and hand it to lost property
questions.why: Found items are logged and handed in to lost property, so that they can be returned to the right owner and nobody is accused. A log protects both staff and guests.

questions.q: Which key rule applies to the master keys Devon uses?
o: Leave them on the trolley so that they are easy to find in the corridor
Lend them to a colleague if it saves time on a busy day
Sign them out and in, keep them on your person and never lend them
Keep a spare copy in a drawer at the front desk for emergencies
questions.why: A master key opens many rooms, so a lost or lent key puts all guests at risk. Control the key by signing it in and out, and report a loss at once.

questions.q: What should be done about the chicken and rice that have been out for over three hours?
o: Put them in the fridge and serve them again later
Throw them away at once
Reheat them until they are hot and serve them again
Cover them with foil and leave them in the shade
questions.why: Cooked food left in the danger zone (between about 5 °C and 63 °C) for more than about two hours may carry harmful germs, and reheating may not make it safe. Throw it away.

questions.q: How should Marlon deal with the cut on his finger?
o: Leave it uncovered, because it is only a small cut
Cover it with a blue plaster and a glove
Cover it with a paper tissue that is held in place with tape
Wipe it with a cloth and continue working
questions.why: A blue waterproof plaster is easy to see if it falls into food, and a glove over it keeps germs from the cut out of food.

questions.q: What should the helper have done before slicing the tomatoes?
o: Washed his hands and used a clean board and knife
Wiped the same board with a damp cloth and carried on
Rinsed the knife in cold water and used the same board
Sliced the tomatoes on the same board but on the clean side
questions.why: Raw chicken carries harmful germs. Using the same board or knife would pass them to tomatoes that are not cooked again, which is cross-contamination.

questions.q: A kitchen swaps a strong acid cleaner for a milder one that does the same job. In the hierarchy of control, which step is this?
o: Elimination
Administrative control
Personal protective equipment
Substitution
questions.why: Substitution means replacing a hazardous thing with a safer one. Elimination would remove the need for the cleaner, administrative controls are rules and training, and PPE protects the worker only.

questions.q: When using a fire extinguisher, what does the 'A' in PASS tell you to do?
o: Attack the top of the flames first, where the fire is biggest
Aim at the tallest part of the smoke above the flames
Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire
Alert all of the guests before you start to fight the fire
questions.why: The fire burns at its base, where the fuel is, so you aim there. PASS is Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze the handle, Sweep from side to side.
